steps.question: Staff want a helper that answers from the city's own handbook and shows which pages it used. Which Bedrock feature fits?

options.text: Knowledge Bases, which look up the right handbook passages first (RAG)

options.text: Guardrails
options.why: Guardrails filter what goes in and out, like denied topics. They don't give the model your handbook.

options.text: Batch inference
options.why: Batch runs lots of prompts later, from files in S3. It doesn't look anything up in your documents.

quests.title: The Machine Shop
quests.intro: Every machine on my factory floor is rented by the second. Pick the right size and the right deal, and you never pay for idle steel.

steps.text: Walk to the EC2 Factory and meet Eddie
Learn 5 EC2 cards, like instance types, AMIs and pricing options
Hands on: make a key pair, the first step of the EC2 workshop
Help a website survive its Friday rush
steps.question: A team's website runs on one EC2 server. Traffic doubles every Friday evening, then drops for the rest of the week. What keeps it fast without paying for big servers all week?

options.text: An Auto Scaling group that adds servers when it gets busy and removes them after
options.why: It scales out for the rush and back in afterwards, so you pay only for the servers that are running.

options.text: Buy the biggest instance size and leave it on all week
options.why: That pays for Friday-night capacity every hour of every day.

options.text: Turn on termination protection
options.why: That only stops someone deleting the server by mistake. It adds no capacity.

steps.text: Pick the cheapest way to run a batch job
steps.question: A nightly batch job can be stopped and restarted without harm. Which way of buying EC2 capacity costs the least?

options.text: Spot Instances
options.why: Spare EC2 capacity at a large discount. AWS can take it back with a two-minute warning, which an interruptible job can handle.

options.text: On-Demand Instances
options.why: Full price by the second, with no commitment. Right for work that must not be interrupted.

options.text: Dedicated Hosts
options.why: A whole physical server just for you: useful for some software licences, and the most expensive option here.

quests.title: Kube's Harbour
quests.intro: Kubernetes is the shipping system half the world already uses. I run its control tower for you; you bring the ships.

steps.text: Walk to the EKS Harbour Tower and meet Kube
Learn 4 EKS cards about clusters, pods and nodes
Find out what Kube runs for you
steps.question: When you create an Amazon EKS cluster, what does AWS run and look after for you?

options.text: The Kubernetes control plane, spread across several Availability Zones
options.why: AWS runs and patches the control plane. Your pods still run on nodes: EC2 servers, or AWS Fargate.

options.text: Your containers, with no nodes or capacity needed at all
options.why: Pods need somewhere to run: EC2 nodes, managed node groups or AWS Fargate.

options.text: A new image format that replaces your container images
options.why: You still build ordinary container images. EKS runs standard Kubernetes.

steps.text: Choose between two container harbours
steps.question: A team already runs Kubernetes in its own data centre and wants to keep the same tools and skills on AWS. Which service fits best?

options.text: Amazon EKS
options.why: It runs standard, upstream Kubernetes, so the team keeps its tools, manifests and know-how.

options.text: Amazon ECS
options.why: A simpler AWS container service, but it isn't Kubernetes: the team would learn a new way of working.

options.text: AWS Lambda
options.why: Functions that run on demand. Good for events, but not a place to run a Kubernetes setup.

steps.text: Learn 2 EBS cards about disks that attach to one server
Learn 2 EFS cards about one folder many servers share
Give Kube's pods their own disks and one shared folder

quests.title: Plant It and Grow
quests.intro: Bring me your code and I'll grow everything around it: servers, a load balancer, scaling and health checks. You can still look under the leaves.

steps.text: Walk to Beanstalk Garden and meet Jack
Learn 4 Elastic Beanstalk cards about environments and deploys
Pick a home for a small web app
steps.question: A student has a small web app. They don't want to set up servers, load balancers and scaling by hand, but they want to see the servers that run it. Which service fits?

options.text: AWS Elastic Beanstalk
options.why: Upload the code and it creates the EC2 servers, load balancer and scaling for you, and you can still open every one of them.

options.text: Amazon Redshift
options.why: A data warehouse for analysing huge tables. It doesn't host web apps.

options.text: AWS KMS
options.why: It looks after encryption keys. It doesn't run code.

steps.text: Find out what Beanstalk itself costs
steps.question: What do you pay for Elastic Beanstalk itself?

options.text: Nothing extra: you pay only for the resources it creates, like EC2 servers and the load balancer
options.why: Beanstalk has no charge of its own. Turn the environment off and its servers stop costing money.

options.text: A monthly fee per app, on top of the servers
options.why: There's no extra fee for Beanstalk itself.

options.text: A charge for every deploy
options.why: Deploys are free; you pay for what runs.

steps.text: Learn 2 RDS cards about managed databases with backups
Design the Garden Club Sign-ups app with its own database

quests.title: Bex's Lockers
quests.intro: Each locker sits in one Availability Zone and plugs into a server there. Fast and private, but remember where it lives.

steps.text: Walk to the EBS Lockers and meet Bex
Learn 4 EBS cards about volumes, types and snapshots
Move a locker to another zone
steps.question: An EBS volume is in us-east-1a. Can a server in us-east-1b attach it?

options.text: No. A volume attaches only to servers in its own Availability Zone; take a snapshot and create a new volume there
options.why: Volumes live in one zone. A snapshot can make a copy in any zone of the Region, or be copied to another Region.

options.text: Yes, any server in the same Region can attach it
options.why: Volumes are tied to one Availability Zone.

options.text: Only if the volume is encrypted
options.why: Encryption protects the data; it doesn't change where the volume can attach.

steps.text: Keep a locker safe from a bad day
steps.question: How do you protect an EBS volume's data in case its Availability Zone has a problem?

options.text: Take regular snapshots (Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager can automate them)
options.why: Snapshots are stored across the Region, so you can rebuild the volume in another zone. Copy them to another Region for even more safety.

options.text: Make the volume bigger
options.why: More space doesn't make a second copy anywhere.

options.text: Attach the volume to two servers
options.why: Even where that's possible, both servers are in the same zone, so it doesn't help if that zone fails.

quests.title: The Shared Well
quests.intro: One well, many buckets dipping in at once. Servers in every zone draw the same water from me.

steps.text: Walk to the EFS Shared Well and meet Effie
Learn 4 EFS cards about shared file systems and storage classes
Give ten servers the same files
steps.question: Ten web servers in different Availability Zones must read and write the same files at the same time. Which storage fits?

options.text: Amazon EFS
options.why: A shared file system that many servers mount at once, across Availability Zones.

options.text: Amazon EBS
options.why: A volume lives in one Availability Zone and usually belongs to one server.

options.text: The server's own instance store
options.why: Fast, but the data disappears when the server stops, and no other server can see it.

steps.text: Pay less for files nobody opens
steps.question: Most files in a file system haven't been opened for months. How do you pay less without deleting them?

options.text: Turn on lifecycle management so EFS moves them to the Infrequent Access or Archive storage class
options.why: EFS moves cold files to cheaper classes automatically and brings them back when they're opened.

options.text: Copy them to an EBS volume
options.why: That adds a second bill and loses the sharing.

options.text: Make the file system read-only
options.why: That stops changes but doesn't make storage cheaper.

quests.title: Ray's Records Hall
quests.intro: Rows and columns, kept tidy. I patch the engine, take the backups and keep a standby ready, so you can get on with your app.

steps.text: Walk to the RDS Records Hall and meet Ray
Learn 5 RDS cards about engines, backups and Multi-AZ
Hands on: create a practice database in the RDS workshop
Keep the ledgers open if a building fails
steps.question: What does a Multi-AZ deployment do for an RDS database?

options.text: Keeps a standby copy in another Availability Zone and fails over to it automatically
options.why: If the main database or its zone fails, RDS switches to the standby, usually within a minute or two.

options.text: Copies data to another Region to make reads faster there
options.why: That's a cross-Region read replica, a different feature.

options.text: Makes every query run faster
options.why: The standby is for failover. It doesn't speed up queries.

steps.text: Help a database that reads all day
steps.question: An app reads far more than it writes, and the database is getting busy. What helps most?

options.text: Add read replicas and send the reads to them
options.why: Replicas take copies of the data and answer read queries, so the main database has more room for writes.

options.text: Turn off automated backups
options.why: That removes your safety net and barely helps performance.

options.text: Move the database to a smaller instance
options.why: Less capacity makes a busy database slower.

quests.title: Reggie's Big Questions
quests.intro: Billions of rows, stacked in columns. Ask me something big, like ten years of sales by month, and I'll answer before your tea cools.

steps.text: Walk to the Redshift Warehouse and meet Reggie
Learn 4 Redshift cards about warehouses and columns
Pick the right job for the warehouse
steps.question: Which job suits Amazon Redshift best?

options.text: Analysing billions of sales rows to find trends across years
options.why: That's analytics (OLAP): big scans over many rows, which is what a data warehouse is built for.

options.text: Saving each shopping-cart click within milliseconds
options.why: Lots of tiny, fast writes (OLTP) suit a database like DynamoDB.

options.text: Storing customers' profile photos
options.why: Files and photos belong in Amazon S3.

steps.text: Find out why columns are fast
steps.question: Why does Redshift store data by column rather than by row?

options.text: A question about a few columns reads only those columns, so big scans are faster and compress better
options.why: Values in a column are alike, so they compress well, and unused columns are never read.

options.text: So each row can be updated faster
options.why: Single-row updates are what row-based databases do best.

options.text: Because columns never need backups
options.why: Redshift still takes snapshots of your data.

steps.text: Design the Treasury's Ledger: join old files with new sales

quests.title: Nep's Web
quests.intro: Who knows whom, who bought what, what links to what: I keep the threads, so you can walk from one to the next.

steps.text: Walk to Neptune Web and meet Nep
Learn 4 Neptune cards about graphs, nodes and edges
Pick a question for a graph
steps.question: Which question is a graph database like Amazon Neptune best at?

options.text: Which friends of my friends bought this book?
options.why: Following links between people and things, hop after hop, is what graphs are made for.

options.text: What were our total sales last year?
options.why: A big sum over many rows is a job for a data warehouse like Redshift.

options.text: Where should I store this video file?
options.why: Files belong in Amazon S3.

steps.text: Learn how to ask Nep a question
steps.question: Which query languages can you use with Amazon Neptune?

options.text: Graph query languages such as Gremlin and openCypher
options.why: Neptune answers graph questions in graph languages (it also speaks one made for linked web data), not in SQL.

options.text: Only SQL
options.why: Neptune is a graph database; it speaks graph query languages, not SQL.

options.text: Spreadsheet formulas
options.why: Spreadsheets are for tables, not graphs.

steps.text: Design Who Knows Whom: follow the links between accounts

quests.title: Sage's Workbench
quests.intro: Some models you borrow; some you build. In my workshop you bring the data, train the model and send it out to answer questions.

steps.text: Walk to the SageMaker Workshop and meet Sage
Learn 4 SageMaker AI cards about training and endpoints
Choose between building and borrowing a model
steps.question: When would you pick Amazon SageMaker AI over Amazon Bedrock?

options.text: When you want to train or tune your own model on your own data and control the training
options.why: SageMaker AI gives you the tools to build, train and deploy models yourself.

options.text: When you just want to call a ready-made foundation model through an API
options.why: That's Amazon Bedrock: no training or servers to manage.

options.text: When you need to store training files
options.why: Training data usually lives in Amazon S3, whichever service trains the model.

steps.text: Put a trained model to work
steps.question: A trained model must answer requests from your app all day. What do you create in SageMaker AI?

options.text: A real-time inference endpoint
options.why: An endpoint keeps the model loaded and answers each request as it arrives.

options.text: A training job
options.why: A training job builds the model, then stops. It doesn't answer requests.

options.text: A notebook
options.why: Notebooks are for exploring data and experimenting, not for serving an app.

steps.text: Design the Clinic Model Lab with a key the clinic controls

quests.title: Ask Quill
quests.intro: Stuck on an error? Lost in the console? Ask me where you work. I'll explain, suggest and point you to the docs, and you stay in charge.

steps.text: Walk to the Q Help Desk and meet Quill
Learn 4 Amazon Q cards about asking for help where you work
Get help with a confusing error
steps.question: Your Lambda function fails in the AWS console with an error you don't understand. How can Amazon Q help?

options.text: Ask Amazon Q in the console to explain the error and suggest how to fix it
options.why: Amazon Q can help diagnose console errors and explain them in plain words, right where you are.

options.text: It quietly changes your resources to fix the error
options.why: Amazon Q explains and suggests; you decide what to change.

options.text: It deletes the function and starts again
options.why: That would lose your code. Q helps you understand the problem instead.

steps.text: Decide how much to trust an assistant
steps.question: Is everything an AI assistant like Amazon Q says always right?

options.text: No. Check its answers, as you would anyone's, before you change anything important
options.why: AI assistants can be wrong. Read the suggestion, check the docs it links, and test changes safely.

options.text: Yes, it can't make mistakes
options.why: Every AI assistant can make mistakes.

options.text: Only on weekends
options.why: Mistakes don't keep a calendar. Always check.

steps.text: Send alarms to the team chat, where Quill answers questions

quests.title: Rex's Gallery
quests.intro: Every picture that comes through my doors gets a look: what's in it, whether it's safe, and whose face it might be in your own collection.

steps.text: Walk to the Rekognition Gallery and meet Rex
Learn 4 Rekognition cards about labels, faces and moderation
Keep unsafe pictures off an app
steps.question: A photo-sharing app must stop unsafe images before other people see them. Which service checks the images?

options.text: Amazon Rekognition content moderation
options.why: It labels unsafe or inappropriate content, so the app can hide an image or send it for a person to review.

options.text: Amazon Textract
options.why: Textract reads text and forms from documents. It doesn't judge images.

options.text: Amazon EFS
options.why: EFS stores files; it doesn't look at them.

steps.text: Find the same person in many photos
steps.question: A family photo app wants to find every picture of one person across thousands of photos. What does Rekognition offer?

options.text: Face search: index the faces into a collection, then search it with a photo
options.why: Rekognition compares faces against the collection you built, with a similarity score for each match.

options.text: It reads the names printed on everyone's clothes
options.why: That's not how face search works; it compares faces.

options.text: It turns each photo into a spreadsheet
options.why: Spreadsheets aren't involved. Rekognition returns faces, labels and scores.

quests.title: Tex Reads the Forms
quests.intro: Scanned pages, crooked tables, boxes filled in by hand: bring them to my scriptorium and I'll copy out what matters.

steps.text: Walk to the Textract Scriptorium and meet Tex
Learn 4 Textract cards about text, tables and forms
Save a clinic from retyping forms
steps.question: A clinic has thousands of scanned forms, and staff retype the name and date boxes by hand. What can Amazon Textract do?

options.text: Read the forms and return each field as a key and value, plus tables and text
options.why: Textract finds form fields, tables and lines of text, so an app can file them without retyping.

options.text: Translate the forms into other languages
options.why: Translation is Amazon Translate's job.

options.text: Store the scans cheaply
options.why: Storing files is a job for Amazon S3.

steps.text: Handle a messy handwritten box
steps.question: Textract isn't sure about one handwritten field. What should the app do?

options.text: Check the confidence score Textract returns, and send unsure fields to a person to review
options.why: Every result comes with a confidence score. Low scores are the ones a person should check.

options.text: Accept every answer as it comes
options.why: Unchecked mistakes end up in the clinic's records.

options.text: Throw the whole form away
options.why: One unclear box doesn't make the rest of the form wrong.

steps.text: Design the Claims Desk: check photos and read forms

quests.title: The Red Team Range
quests.intro: I attack your apps before anyone else can, but only the ones you own. Let's set up a fair, safe test and learn to read what I find.

steps.text: Walk to the Red Team Range and meet Rhea
Learn 5 Security Agent cards, like scope, proof and pricing
Agree which sites Rhea may test
steps.question: A team wants Rhea to pen test shop.example.com. What has to happen before the test can start?

options.text: They prove they own the domain, for example with a record in its DNS
options.why: AWS Security Agent only tests domains you've proven you own, with a record in its DNS or a check page on the site.

options.text: Nothing: any website can be tested
options.why: Testing sites you don't own isn't allowed, and the agent refuses domains that aren't verified.

options.text: They email AWS a screenshot of the site
options.why: Ownership is proven technically, with a DNS record or a check page, not with a picture.

steps.text: Keep the test from doing real harm
steps.question: Which page should be marked out of scope before a pen test?

options.text: The page that bulk-deletes customer orders
options.why: Destructive or irreversible actions, like bulk deletes, payments and sending messages, belong out of scope.

options.text: The product search page
options.why: Search is a normal page worth testing. Injection flaws often hide behind search boxes.

options.text: The public home page
options.why: The home page is safe to test, and attackers see it first.

steps.text: Choose where to point the test
steps.question: Where should the team run its pen test?

options.text: A pre-production copy that closely mirrors the live app
options.why: Even careful test attacks can trip real business rules, so AWS recommends testing pre-production.

options.text: The live site, during the busiest sale of the year
options.why: Real customers and their data could be affected, at the worst possible moment.

options.text: A blank page with none of the app's code
options.why: A test only finds flaws in the app it can reach. An empty page has nothing to find.

steps.text: Plan a fair practice attack on a copy of the shop

steps.prompt: What does AWS Security Agent include with each penetration test finding?
steps.text: Ask the agents what a good finding looks like

quests.title: Agents at Work
quests.intro: An agent is a microservice with a mind of its own. Let's give yours good tools, helpful friends and firm limits, so it grows without surprises.

steps.text: Walk to the AgentCore Academy and talk to Ace
Learn 10 AgentCore cards, like sessions, Gateway tools and A2A
Give an agent the right tool
steps.question: An agent needs to call the shop's order service. What's a good way to give it that tool?

options.text: Put the order service behind AgentCore Gateway as an MCP tool
options.why: Gateway turns Lambda functions and APIs into MCP tools that agents can find and call.

options.text: Paste the database password into the agent's prompt
options.why: Secrets in prompts can leak. The agent should go through a tool with its own permissions.

options.text: Let the agent guess the service's web address
options.why: Guessing makes calls unpredictable. A tool should be named and described.

steps.text: Plan for a tool called twice
steps.question: A model may call the same tool twice, or stop halfway. How should the order tool behave?

options.text: Make it idempotent: a repeat call with the same order number changes nothing
options.why: Models call tools unpredictably. An idempotent tool stays correct when a call repeats.

options.text: Assume each tool is called exactly once
options.why: Retries happen, so a second call could place the same order twice.

options.text: Block the agent after its first call
options.why: That stops legitimate retries too. Making repeats safe is better.

steps.text: Split a crowded agent
steps.question: One agent has 40 tools and keeps picking the wrong one. What helps most?

options.text: Split it into specialised agents that hand work to each other, for example over A2A
options.why: Fewer tools per agent means clearer choices, and AgentCore Runtime can host A2A agents.

options.text: Give it 20 more tools
options.why: A longer list dilutes the model's choices even more.

options.text: Remove the model and keep the tools
options.why: Then nothing decides which tool to use.

steps.prompt: How do AgentCore Runtime sessions keep one user's agent work apart from another's?
steps.text: Ask the agents how sessions stay apart

quests.title: Remy's Last Relay
quests.intro: I've run thousands of web apps straight from code or containers. App Runner takes no new customers now, so my last race is passing the baton safely to ECS Express Mode.

steps.text: Walk to the App Runner Relay Track and meet Remy
Learn 4 App Runner cards about sources, scaling and the handover
Help a new team pick its starting line
steps.question: A team new to AWS wants to run a web app from one container image, with HTTPS and scaling handled for them. What does AWS recommend now?

options.text: Amazon ECS Express Mode
options.why: From one image and two roles it builds an ECS service on Fargate, a load balancer, scaling and networking.

options.text: AWS App Runner
options.why: App Runner is closed to new customers. Only teams already using it can create services.

options.text: One EC2 server they patch themselves
options.why: It can work, but they'd set up scaling, the load balancer and patching on their own.

steps.text: Learn 2 ECS cards about services and tasks
Learn 2 Route 53 cards about records and routing
Plan a move with a quick way back
steps.question: The bakery site on App Runner uses its own domain. How do you move it to ECS Express Mode and keep a quick way back?

options.text: Route 53 weighted records: shift 10, then 25, 50, 75 and 100 percent
options.why: Both run side by side, so switching back is just a weight change while App Runner is still up.

options.text: Delete App Runner first, then create the new service
options.why: Visitors get errors in between, and there's nothing to switch back to.

options.text: Point the domain at the new service all at once
options.why: It can work, but any problem hits every visitor at once.

steps.text: Design Remy's baton handover

quests.title: Bram's Night Shift
quests.intro: Some work doesn't need an answer this second, just by morning. Give me a pile of orders and I'll light exactly enough ovens to bake them all.

steps.text: Walk to the Batch Bakery and meet Bram
Learn 4 Batch cards about jobs, queues and compute environments
Pick the right kitchen for a long bake
steps.question: Each video frame takes about an hour to render, and there are 5,000 of them. Which service fits best?

options.text: AWS Batch
options.why: An array job fans out into thousands of child jobs on capacity that scales to the queue.

options.text: AWS Lambda
options.why: One run stops after 15 minutes, and each frame takes an hour.

options.text: Amazon Lightsail
options.why: Fixed-price servers you'd share the frames out to by hand, paid for busy or idle.

steps.text: Make the night shift cheaper
steps.question: The renders can start again if they are interrupted. How do you pay less for the compute?

options.text: A Spot compute environment, with a retry strategy for interrupted jobs
options.why: Spare capacity at a steep discount, and retries rerun any job whose capacity is taken back.

options.text: Keep a large On-Demand fleet running all day
options.why: You'd pay for idle servers between batches.

options.text: Give each job more memory
options.why: More memory makes each job cost more, not less.

steps.text: Learn 2 EventBridge cards about rules and targets
Design Bram's overnight render bake

quests.title: Skye's Easy Moorings
quests.intro: Not everyone needs a whole shipyard. I rent ready-rigged boats for one monthly price, and you can sail from day one.

steps.text: Walk to the Lightsail Marina and meet Skye
Learn 4 Lightsail cards about plans, images and static addresses
Help the sailing club choose a host
steps.question: A small club wants a WordPress site for a fixed, predictable monthly price, with as little setup as possible. Which fits?

options.text: Amazon Lightsail
options.why: A WordPress image and one monthly plan with storage and data transfer included.

options.text: Amazon EC2 with a load balancer and RDS
options.why: Powerful and flexible, but more to set up, and the bill changes with use.

options.text: AWS Batch
options.why: Batch runs jobs that finish. A website must answer visitors all day.

steps.text: Keep the address after a restart
steps.question: The club's site moved to a new address after the instance was stopped and started. What prevents this?

options.text: Attach a static IP address to the instance
options.why: It stays the same across restarts and costs nothing while attached.

options.text: Take a snapshot every day
options.why: Snapshots back up the disk. They don't keep the public address.

options.text: Open port 443 in the firewall
options.why: That lets HTTPS in, but the address would still change.

steps.text: Learn 2 Route 53 cards about pointing a domain at a site
Design the sailing club's blog

quests.title: Bea's Strongroom
quests.intro: Things get deleted, broken or locked away by mistake. I keep a copy of everything on a timetable, and nobody opens my strongroom early.

steps.text: Walk to the Backup Storehouse and meet Bea
Learn 4 Backup cards about plans, vaults and recovery points
Replace a pile of backup scripts
steps.question: A team backs up DynamoDB, EFS and EBS with three different scripts. What gives them one schedule and one place to check?

options.text: One AWS Backup plan, assigned by tag
options.why: One plan backs up all three on a schedule and shows every job in one console.

options.text: Turn on S3 versioning
options.why: Versioning keeps old versions of objects in a bucket. It doesn't back up tables, file systems or disks.

options.text: A bigger EBS volume
options.why: More space on the same disk is not a separate copy you can restore.

steps.text: Stop early deletion, even by admins
steps.question: Auditors need proof that nobody, not even the root user, can delete backups before a year is up. What do you use?

options.text: Vault Lock in compliance mode
options.why: After its grace time of at least 72 hours, no one can delete backups early or change the lock.

options.text: Vault Lock in governance mode
options.why: Users with enough IAM permissions can still remove a governance lock.

options.text: An IAM policy that denies deletion
options.why: An admin who can edit IAM policies could simply remove it again.

steps.text: Learn 2 EBS cards about disks and snapshots
Design Bea's locked backup plan

quests.title: Kenzie's Millrace
quests.intro: Data that's an hour old is too late for some jobs. My millrace carries every record as it happens, in order, to every wheel that needs it.

steps.text: Walk to the Kinesis Water Mill and meet Kenzie
Learn 4 Kinesis cards about shards, keys and retention
Choose between a stream and a queue
steps.question: Two separate apps must each read every click, in order for each player, and read the last day again if they fail. Which fits?

options.text: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams
options.why: Many apps read the same stream on their own, in order per partition key, and can read again within retention.

options.text: An Amazon SQS standard queue
options.why: Each message goes to one consumer and is deleted once processed, and order is not guaranteed.

options.text: An Amazon S3 bucket
options.why: Good for keeping raw clicks, but apps can't read them in order as they arrive.

steps.text: Keep each player's clicks in order
steps.question: Which partition key keeps each player's clicks in order and spreads the load across shards?

options.text: The player's id
options.why: Same player, same shard, so their clicks stay in order, and many players spread the load.

options.text: Today's date
options.why: Every record that day shares one key and lands on one shard: a hot spot.

options.text: A random number for each record
options.why: The load spreads, but one player's clicks scatter across shards and lose their order.

steps.text: Learn 2 Lambda cards about functions and triggers
Design Kenzie's live scoreboard

quests.title: Ola's Index
quests.intro: Every word that comes into my tower gets a note saying where it lives. Ask me for one, and I'll point you to every page that has it.

steps.text: Walk to the OpenSearch Index Tower and meet Ola
Learn 4 OpenSearch cards about domains, shards and search
Pick the right job for the tower
steps.question: Which job suits Amazon OpenSearch Service best?

options.text: Letting shoppers search products by any word in their names and descriptions
options.why: Searching text across many fields is what a search engine is built for.

options.text: Fetching one order by its exact order number
options.why: A lookup by key is DynamoDB's job: fast and cheap at any scale.

options.text: Storing the original product photos
options.why: Files and photos belong in Amazon S3.

steps.text: Size the pieces of a log index
steps.question: A new index will hold about 60 GiB of logs, which is write-heavy work. Roughly how big should each shard be?

options.text: About 30 to 50 GiB
options.why: For write-heavy work such as log analytics, AWS suggests shards of about 30 to 50 GiB.

options.text: As small as possible, like 1 GiB
options.why: Too many small shards use up processing power and memory, and can slow the whole cluster.

options.text: One single 60 GiB shard, with more added later
options.why: Very large shards are slow to recover, and adding primary shards to an index later is hard.

steps.text: Design Product Search: find any item by any word

quests.title: Doc's Archive
quests.intro: Every folder in my archive is shaped its own way: one has three pages, the next has thirty. Bring me any folder and I'll file it, then find it again by anything inside.

steps.text: Walk to the DocumentDB Archive and meet Doc
Learn 4 DocumentDB cards about documents, copies and backups
Pick data for the archive
steps.question: Which data suits a document database like Amazon DocumentDB best?

options.text: User profiles where every user shares different details
options.why: Documents can each hold different fields, so each profile stores only what that user gave.

options.text: Ten years of sales to add up by month
options.why: Big sums over many rows are a job for a data warehouse like Redshift.

options.text: Which friends of friends bought this book
options.why: Following links hop after hop is what a graph database like Neptune is for.

steps.text: Move an app without rewriting it
steps.question: A team's app already uses MongoDB drivers. They want a managed database on AWS with as few code changes as possible. What fits?

options.text: Amazon DocumentDB
options.why: It's built to run the same application code, drivers and tools used with MongoDB.

options.text: Amazon DynamoDB
options.why: A great database, but it has its own API, so the app's data code would need rewriting.

options.text: Amazon Redshift
options.why: A data warehouse for analytics, not an app's everyday database.

steps.text: Design the Recipe Box: store recipes of every shape

quests.title: Tess's Interchange
quests.intro: Every network's road comes to my interchange. Drive in once, and you can reach any network I'm told to let you reach. No tangle of bridges.

steps.text: Walk to the Transit Gateway Interchange and meet Tess
Learn 4 Transit Gateway cards about hubs and route tables
Find out why pairs aren't enough
steps.question: VPC A is peered with VPC B, and A is also peered with VPC C. Can B reach C through A?

options.text: No: peering isn't transitive, so B and C need their own link, or a hub
options.why: Peering only links pairs. With a transit gateway, every attached network can reach the others it's routed to.

options.text: Yes, traffic hops through A
options.why: Peering never passes traffic on through a third network.

options.text: Only if all three are in different Regions
options.why: Regions don't change it: a peering connection never passes traffic through.

steps.text: Keep the test network apart
steps.question: Test and live networks share one transit gateway. How do you stop test from reaching live?

options.text: Give them separate route tables with no routes between them
options.why: Each attachment follows one route table, so test can only reach what its table routes to.

options.text: Add a second transit gateway as a spare
options.why: Transit gateways are highly available by design, and a spare doesn't separate traffic.

options.text: Put both in the same subnet
options.why: That would bring them closer together, not keep them apart.

steps.text: Design the Network Interchange: one hub for every network

quests.title: Axel's Express
quests.intro: Two addresses, and they never change. Riders board my express at the stop nearest them, and I drive them to the healthiest Region.

steps.text: Walk to Global Accelerator Express and meet Axel
Learn 4 Global Accelerator cards about fixed addresses and failover
Pick a job for the express
steps.question: Which app needs Global Accelerator rather than CloudFront?

options.text: A game whose players connect straight to game servers, not to web pages
options.why: Global Accelerator carries any kind of traffic to servers in one or more Regions, which suits games and voice calls.

options.text: A blog full of photos for readers worldwide
options.why: Photos and web pages are what CloudFront caches and serves from the edge.

options.text: A video course people stream at home
options.why: CloudFront caches and delivers videos close to viewers.

steps.text: Switch Regions in seconds
steps.question: Partners' firewalls only allow a few fixed IP addresses, and the app must move to another Region fast if one fails. What helps most?

options.text: Global Accelerator's two static IP addresses in front of both Regions
options.why: The addresses never change, so partners allow them once, and new connections move to a healthy Region in seconds.

options.text: Change the DNS record when a Region fails
options.why: Some devices cache old DNS answers for a long time, so users may keep going to the failed Region.

options.text: Give each server its own public IP address
options.why: Partners would have to update their firewalls whenever a server changes.

steps.text: Design the Ticket Express: fixed addresses, fast failover

quests.title: Sid's Strongroom
quests.intro: A password written in the code is a password anyone can read. Bring me your secrets: I'll lock them in the strongroom and change them while you sleep.

steps.text: Walk to the Secrets Manager Strongroom and meet Sid
Learn 4 Secrets Manager cards about storing and rotating secrets
Get a password out of the code
steps.question: A developer pasted the database password into the app's code. What's the safer fix?

options.text: Store it in Secrets Manager, have the app fetch it when it runs, and rotate the old one
options.why: The code no longer holds the password, and rotating it makes the copy that leaked useless.

options.text: Move it into a comment at the bottom of the file
options.why: Anyone who can read the code can still read the comment.

options.text: Email it to the team instead
options.why: Email spreads the password further, and it still never changes.

steps.text: Change the password without a hiccup
steps.question: The payments app must keep working while its database password changes. Which rotation strategy fits?

options.text: Alternating users: two users take turns, so one login always works
options.why: While one user's password changes, the other still works, so the app always gets valid credentials.

options.text: A single user, changed by hand once a year
options.why: Changes by hand are easy to forget, and a single user has a moment where logins can fail.

options.text: Never rotate, in case it breaks something
options.why: A password that never changes stays useful to anyone who ever saw it.

steps.text: Wire the library app to its database with no password in the code

quests.title: Ingrid's Rounds
quests.intro: Every server, container image and function in the city gets a visit from me. When a known flaw turns up, you'll hear about it before an attacker does.

steps.text: Walk to the Inspector's Bureau and meet Ingrid
Learn 4 Inspector cards about scans, flaws and scores
Decide which flaw to fix first
steps.question: Inspector found the same flaw on two servers. One can be reached from the internet, the other can't. Which comes first?

options.text: The one reachable from the internet: its Inspector score is higher
options.why: Inspector adjusts each score to your setup. A flaw attackers can reach from the internet is more urgent.

options.text: Both are equally urgent, so pick one at random
options.why: The same flaw can matter more or less depending on whether attackers can reach it.

options.text: Neither: wait for next year's audit
options.why: Inspector scans all the time so you can fix flaws now, not a year later.

steps.text: Know when Ingrid checks again
steps.question: When does Inspector scan a Lambda function again?

options.text: When the function is updated, or a new flaw that affects it is published
options.why: Inspector rescans on changes and on newly published flaws, with no schedule to set up.

options.text: Only when you press a button each month
options.why: There are no scan schedules to manage: Inspector rescans by itself.

options.text: Never: one scan when it's created is enough
options.why: New flaws are published every day, so an old scan soon goes stale.

quests.title: Mae Follows the Clues
quests.intro: Somewhere in the lake there's a file full of card numbers that shouldn't be there. Let's find it before anyone else does.

steps.text: Walk to the Macie Detective Agency and meet Mae
Learn 4 Macie cards about sensitive data and bucket checks
Spot a bucket left open
steps.question: A bucket of customer records was made public by mistake. Which kind of Macie finding tells you?

options.text: A policy finding about the bucket's public access
options.why: Policy findings report security or privacy problems with a bucket, such as it becoming public.

options.text: A sensitive data finding for each file
options.why: Sensitive data findings report what's inside files, not how the bucket is shared.

options.text: None: Macie only reads the files
options.why: Macie also watches each bucket's access settings and raises policy findings.

steps.text: Search the whole lake on a budget
steps.question: You have hundreds of buckets and want a broad picture of where sensitive data lives. What do you turn on?

options.text: Automated sensitive data discovery, which samples objects in every bucket
options.why: It keeps sampling representative objects everywhere, for a broad view without reading every file.

options.text: A one-off job that reads every object in every bucket
options.why: That works but costs the most. Jobs suit deep checks of the buckets you choose.

options.text: S3 versioning on every bucket
options.why: Versioning keeps old copies of files. It doesn't look for sensitive data.

quests.title: The Control Room
quests.intro: Gwen watches for attackers, Ingrid for flaws, Mae for loose data. My job is to put all their warnings on one board, worst first, and wake the right people.

steps.text: Walk to the Security Hub Control Room and meet Hana
Learn 4 Security Hub cards about findings, checks and scores
Tame a flood of warnings
steps.question: Three watchers each post warnings in their own place, and the team misses the urgent ones. What does Security Hub do?

options.text: Gathers GuardDuty, Inspector and Macie findings in one format and ranks the critical ones
options.why: Security Hub correlates the signals from all three, so the most urgent issues rise to the top.

options.text: Replaces GuardDuty, Inspector and Macie
options.why: Security Hub collects their findings. It still needs them to find threats, flaws and sensitive data.

options.text: Deletes old warnings every night
options.why: Automation rules can suppress or re-rank findings, but its job is to bring them together.

steps.text: Put every warning on one board and wake the team for urgent ones

steps.prompt: What is the difference between GuardDuty, Inspector and Macie?
steps.text: Ask the agents: threats, flaws or sensitive data?

quests.title: Pip Finds a Voice
quests.intro: Hear ye, hear ye! Give me any text and I'll read it aloud in a voice that sounds like a person. Long stories too: I'll leave the recording at the lake.

steps.text: Walk to Polly Speakers' Corner and meet Pip
Learn 4 Polly cards about voices, speech tags and audio
Read a whole chapter aloud
steps.question: A learning app needs a 20-page chapter read aloud as one audio file. How should it ask Polly?

options.text: Start a speech synthesis task that saves the audio file to S3
options.why: Background tasks take up to 100,000 billed characters and save the result in an S3 bucket.

options.text: Send the whole chapter in one SynthesizeSpeech call
options.why: That call is for speech in near real time and stops at 3,000 billed characters.

options.text: Record a person reading it
options.why: That works, but Polly makes the audio in minutes and can redo it whenever the text changes.

steps.text: Make Pip pause and stress a word
steps.question: The quiz app needs a pause before each answer and one word said louder. What does it use?

options.text: Speech tags (SSML) in the text for pauses, volume and emphasis
options.why: Speech Synthesis Markup Language tags tell Polly how to say the text, not just what to say.

options.text: A different voice for every sentence
options.why: Changing voices doesn't add a pause or stress a word.

options.text: Capital letters on the loud word
options.why: Capitals don't set the volume. Speech tags such as emphasis and prosody do.

quests.title: Nora Reads the Room
quests.intro: Ten thousand comments came in overnight. I'll read every one and tell you who's happy, who isn't and what they're talking about.

steps.text: Walk to the Comprehend Reading Room and meet Nora
Learn 4 Comprehend cards about entities, sentiment and personal data
Find out which dish people love
steps.question: Reviews say things like 'The tacos were great but the wait was long'. You want the feeling about each dish. Which feature?

options.text: Targeted sentiment, which scores the feeling about each thing mentioned
options.why: It gives a sentiment for each entity, so the tacos and the wait get separate scores.

options.text: Plain sentiment, one score per review
options.why: One score per review hides that the tacos were loved and the wait wasn't.

options.text: Language detection
options.why: That tells you which language a review is in, not how people feel.

steps.text: Hide personal details
steps.question: Support chats contain phone numbers and home addresses that analysts mustn't see. What can Comprehend do?

options.text: Find the personal details and black them out with an asynchronous job
options.why: Comprehend detects details like addresses and phone numbers, and redaction runs as a batch job.

options.text: Translate the chats into another language
options.why: Translation doesn't remove anyone's phone number.

options.text: Count how many chats mention a product
options.why: That's entity detection. The personal details would still be there.

steps.text: Read every comment's mood and put the kind ones on the radio

quests.title: Stef's Bandstand
quests.intro: Every job is a piece of music. I read the score, cue each player in turn and, if one misses a note, try the bar again. Let's conduct an order from start to finish.

steps.text: Walk to the Step Functions Bandstand and meet Stef
Learn 5 Step Functions cards about states, retries and workflow types
Keep an order going through a short glitch
steps.question: A payment step sometimes fails because the card service is busy for a moment. What should the workflow do?

options.text: Add a Retry with backoff to the payment step, and a Catch for real failures
options.why: Retry tries again after a short, growing wait. Catch sends a failure that keeps happening to the undo steps.

options.text: Nothing: Step Functions retries every step forever by default
options.why: By default an error fails the whole execution. You add Retry yourself.

options.text: Start the whole workflow again from the beginning
options.why: That repeats steps that already worked, like saving the order twice.

steps.text: Pick the right workflow type for payments
steps.question: Which workflow type suits taking payments, where a step must never run twice by accident?

options.text: Standard
options.why: Standard runs each step exactly once unless you add Retry, keeps full history and can run for up to a year.

options.text: Express
options.why: Asynchronous Express runs at least once, so a step could run twice. Better for work that is safe to repeat.

options.text: Either: they behave the same
options.why: They differ in how often steps run, how long a run can last and how they are billed.

steps.text: Design the Bakery Order Line, with undo steps if payment fails

steps.prompt: When should I use AWS Step Functions instead of Amazon EventBridge?
steps.text: Ask the agents: a conductor or a signal box (workflows or events)

quests.title: Draw It Once, Build It Anywhere
quests.intro: Every building in this city started on my drawing board. Write down what you need once, and it gets built the same way every time, in the right order. Even Cody's builds start as my blueprints.

steps.text: Walk to the CloudFormation Blueprint Office and meet Forma
Learn 5 CloudFormation cards about templates, stacks and change sets
Check an update before it builds
steps.question: You're about to rename a database in a stack's template. How do you see what the update will do first?

options.text: Create a change set and read it before running the update
options.why: A change set lists every change. Renaming a database replaces it, so you'd see the risk to its data first.

options.text: Delete the stack and create it again
options.why: That deletes every resource in the stack, data included.

options.text: Rename the database by hand in the console
options.why: Changes made outside CloudFormation cause drift, and the template no longer matches.

steps.text: Find the setting someone changed by hand
steps.question: A teammate changed a server's settings in the EC2 console, not in the template. How can you find what no longer matches?

options.text: Run drift detection on the stack
options.why: It compares each resource's real settings with the template and lists the differences.

options.text: Read the template again
options.why: The template only shows what should be there, not what was changed by hand.

options.text: Create a second stack from the same template
options.why: That builds a new copy. It doesn't check the first one.

steps.text: Draw a design of your own on the Drawing board and get it reviewed
Build a stack from a template (practice is free): one DynamoDB table

quests.title: The Caretaker's Rounds
quests.intro: I look after every machine in town without knocking on a single door. Come on my rounds: we'll patch, run jobs and let the admins in safely.

steps.text: Walk to the Systems Manager Depot and meet Manny
Learn 5 Systems Manager cards about sessions, commands and patches
Let an admin in without opening a door
steps.question: An admin needs a shell on a server in a private subnet. The team wants no open inbound ports and no SSH keys to look after. What fits?

options.text: Session Manager, with IAM deciding who may connect
options.why: It opens the shell through the SSM Agent, with no inbound ports, bastion hosts or SSH keys, and can log every session.

options.text: Open port 22 to the whole internet
options.why: That invites attacks from anywhere, and you still have SSH keys to manage.

options.text: A bastion server in a public subnet
options.why: It works, but it's one more server to patch, pay for and protect.

steps.text: Pick a home for an app's settings
steps.question: An app needs its endpoint address and a feature switch when it starts, without them being written into the code. Where should they live?

options.text: In Parameter Store, part of Systems Manager
options.why: It keeps named settings, plain or encrypted with KMS, and standard parameters cost nothing extra.

options.text: Inside the code, as constants
options.why: Then every change needs a new release, and settings get mixed up with code.

options.text: In the server's name tag
options.why: Tags label resources. They aren't a safe or tidy place for app settings.

steps.text: Design Servers With No Open Doors, patched every week

quests.title: Cora's Survey
quests.intro: I write down how every building in town is set up, and every change since. Tell me the rules, and I'll flag anything that breaks them, even at 3 a.m.

steps.text: Walk to the Config Survey Office and meet Cora
Learn 5 AWS Config cards about records, rules and fixes
Find out what changed, and who changed it
steps.question: A security group's rules changed overnight. Which pair tells you what changed and who changed it?

options.text: AWS Config for the settings before and after, and CloudTrail for who made the call
options.why: Config records each resource's settings over time. CloudTrail records the API call and who made it.

options.text: Amazon GuardDuty on its own
options.why: GuardDuty spots threats. It doesn't keep each resource's settings history.

options.text: Amazon CloudFront logs
options.why: Those record requests to your website, not changes to security groups.

steps.text: Put a broken setting right automatically
steps.question: A Config rule finds a bucket that breaks the rules. How can it be fixed without anyone logging in?

options.text: Attach a remediation action: a Systems Manager Automation runbook that runs automatically
options.why: Config runs the runbook on noncompliant resources, either when you choose or automatically.

options.text: Do nothing: Config rules fix everything on their own
options.why: Rules only check. Remediation actions do the fixing.

options.text: Delete the bucket
options.why: That loses the photos. Remediation changes just the broken setting.

steps.text: Design a fix for The Bucket That Kept Opening

quests.title: The Town Council
quests.intro: One account per team keeps mistakes small, but who keeps all those accounts in order? I do: wards, by-laws and one bill for the whole town.

steps.text: Walk to the Organizations Council House and meet Orla
Learn 5 Organizations cards about accounts, OUs and SCPs
Find out what an SCP can and cannot do
steps.question: A service control policy on a team's OU allows Amazon S3. Can a brand-new role in that account now use S3?

options.text: Only if its IAM policies allow S3 too: an SCP never grants permissions
options.why: SCPs set the most an account can do. The role still needs an IAM policy that allows the action.

options.text: Yes: the SCP gives every role S3 access
options.why: SCPs never grant permissions. They only set limits.

options.text: No: an SCP blocks everything it mentions
options.why: An Allow in an SCP permits the action up to that limit; IAM still decides.

steps.text: Choose where the teams' apps should run
steps.question: Where should the teams' apps and data live?

options.text: In member accounts, not the management account
options.why: SCPs don't restrict the management account, so AWS recommends keeping resources out of it.

options.text: In the management account, to keep the bill simple
options.why: Member accounts already share one bill through consolidated billing.

options.text: All together in one account
options.why: Separate accounts keep each team's mistakes, permissions and costs apart.

steps.text: Design Every New Account, Ready, with one audit trail for all

quests.title: Gracie's Switchboard
quests.intro: Ask me for exactly what you need. I'll ring every source on one line, and the moment anything changes, I'll ring you back.

steps.text: Walk to the AppSync Switchboard and meet Gracie
Learn 5 AppSync cards about GraphQL, resolvers and live updates
Pick an API for a busy phone app
steps.question: A phone app's home screen needs a user's profile, their orders and today's offers, which live in three places, in a single request. Which fits best?

options.text: AWS AppSync, with a GraphQL API
options.why: One GraphQL request can ask for exactly those fields from several data sources at once.

options.text: Amazon SQS
options.why: A queue passes messages between back-end parts. It doesn't answer an app's request.

options.text: Amazon Redshift
options.why: A data warehouse for big analysis, not quick answers for a phone app.

steps.text: Make the app update by itself
steps.question: How can the app show a new order the moment it is saved, without asking the server every few seconds?

options.text: A GraphQL subscription, which AppSync triggers when a mutation saves the order
options.why: AppSync keeps a WebSocket connection open and pushes each change to subscribed apps.

options.text: Ask the server again every second
options.why: Constant asking wastes requests and battery, and still lags behind.

options.text: Email the user each change
options.why: Email is slow and leaves the screen out of date.

steps.text: Design Sports Day Live, with scores pushed to every phone

steps.prompt: When should I pick AWS AppSync instead of Amazon API Gateway?
steps.text: Ask the agents: when one switchboard line beats many ticket counters
